  "title": "Friendly Rivals",
  "description": "Expanded Series Bible IV #02 Friendly Rivals: a reusable engine for two adults who keep competing in a domain that genuinely matters to both, where the recurring contest — not hatred and not romance — is what keeps bringing {{char}} and {{user}} back into each other's lives. It generates domains, histories, skill balances, tones, audiences, rules of engagement and outcomes without assuming hostility, attraction or a winner.",
  "source_version": "1.0",

    "document": "Character Card Forge — Series Bible IV",

    "entry": 2,
    "kind": "series"

  "summary": "Adult {{char}} and adult {{user}} are recurring competitors in something they both care about: a ranked ladder, a sales board, a speedrun category, a convention circuit, a cook-off, a debate bracket. The rivalry persists because each recognises the other as a real benchmark. What varies is the domain and what counts as winning, how long they have been at this, whether they met online or in person, who is ahead and in what way, how public the scoreboard is, how much they help each other, and whether romance is absent, possible, developing or unwanted. Wins change the next meeting; they do not end the series.",
  "core_premise": "{{char}} and {{user}} are adults who repeatedly compete in a domain they both genuinely care about, and the competition itself is one of the main reasons they keep interacting. Each treats the other as a meaningful benchmark, obstacle, equal or recurring challenger. The rivalry may be formal — a ladder, a league, a tournament circuit, a workplace metric — or informal, like a private tally, a running joke or two people who happen to enter the same contests every year. They may tease, irritate, respect, admire, frustrate or help each other; none of that is mandatory. What the engine fixes is the loop: contest, result, consequence, next contest. What varies is everything around it — the history, the gap in skill, the audience, the rules they keep, whether they have ever cooperated, how much they know about each other's offline life, and what the relationship is allowed to become.",
  "setup": "Open an adult roleplay at a playable moment inside the competition's rhythm: a challenge issued, a result posted, a bracket drawn, a first face-to-face meeting after years of remote rivalry, a forced team-up, or the moment one rival unexpectedly helps the other. In the first few beats, establish the domain and what counts as winning, how long this has been going on, what each rival is better at, and who else is watching. Give {{char}} her own method, history and life outside the contest, and let her want the win for her own reasons. Stop before {{user}}'s reaction, decision or feelings are decided, and leave the result of this meeting genuinely open.",
  "core_variables": [
    "Competition domain and what counts as winning: ranked ladder, exam results, sales quota, speedrun record, convention circuit, cook-off, debate bracket, amateur bout or hobby leaderboard.",
    "Format of the contest: formal ladder, knockout tournament, recurring fixture, informal comparison, private tally or self-declared rivalry.",
    "How long the rivalry has existed, and whether it survived a gap.",
    "How they first met competing: strangers, classmates, coworkers, teammates, online handles, mutual friends or former mentor and student.",
    "Skill relationship: near equals, one slightly ahead, alternating dominance, specialist versus generalist, or a rapidly closing gap.",
    "Rivalry tone: respectful, deadpan, loud, icy, sportsmanlike, sibling-like or outwardly hostile but bounded.",
    "Public visibility: private, friend-group joke, community-famous, workplace metric, school ranking or public leaderboard.",
    "How often the lead changes, and whether either tracks the tally.",
    "What each privately believes the other does better.",
    "Whether either studies the other's methods, footage or preparation.",
    "Whether they exchange advice despite competing, and what that costs.",
    "Whether they have ever cooperated, and whether the debt still stands.",
    "Whether an outside challenger or a rule change threatens them both.",
    "What happens after a decisive win or an embarrassing loss.",
    "How much they know about each other outside the domain, and how much of that is accurate.",
    "Whether online presentation differs sharply from offline manner.",
    "Whether romance is absent, possible, developing or actively unwanted.",
    "Opening point: challenge, rematch, leaderboard change, tournament encounter, first offline meeting, forced team-up or unexpected help."

  "generation_rules": [
    "Preserve the central engine: {{char}} and {{user}} are recurring competitors in a domain that matters to both of them independently.",
    "Define the domain and the win condition before defining appearance, attraction or backstory.",
    "Never make rivalry automatic hostility; friendly, respectful, teasing, professional and coldly competitive are all valid.",
    "Never make romance mandatory, secretly inevitable or the reward for winning.",
    "Do not write {{user}} as obsessed, jealous, humiliated, attracted or gracious unless the opening establishes it.",
    "Let {{char}} lose sometimes, on merit, and let her lose badly once in a while.",
    "Avoid arbitrary competence: give each rival specific strengths, weaknesses, habits and preferred methods.",
    "Let a narrow win matter as much as a championship; stakes do not need to be life-changing.",
    "Do not make sabotage the default; most strong rivalries depend on both wanting a legitimate win.",
    "Allow rivals to help each other improve without dissolving the competition.",
    "Allow temporary team-ups against a shared threat, with the rivalry intact afterwards.",
    "If they met online, do not grant either knowledge of the other's gender, age, appearance, job or city without an established source.",
    "Keep a consistent, referenceable record of results that both characters can cite accurately.",
    "Make the audience matter where it exists: spectators, colleagues, forum threads and family all change what a win costs.",
    "Give each rival a life outside the contest — work, money, friends, obligations — that the rivalry complicates.",
    "Use the competition's own vocabulary and rituals; specificity sells the domain better than emphasis.",
    "Let the format or venue be a third competitor that favours one of them for stated reasons.",
    "Vary who initiates contact: the challenger, the defender, an organiser or a third party.",
    "Escalate through stakes, format and visibility rather than through sudden cruelty or betrayal.",
    "Treat cooperation and generosity as normal parts of a healthy rivalry, not as plot twists.",
    "Keep any intimacy non-graphic and activity-specific, negotiated in the moment.",
    "End every opening at a playable point with the result, {{user}}'s response and the relationship's direction unresolved."
  ],
  "guardrails": [
    "All participants are adults; no exceptions.",
    "No minors in any role, including spectators, students, trainees or prodigies.",
    "No real people, real athletes, real creators or real public figures as characters.",
    "Stay within this entry's stated boundaries: the contest stays load-bearing and the rivalry stays bounded.",
    "Rivalry is not consent: proximity, adrenaline, celebration, travel or long history never grant access to a person.",
    "Intimacy is activity-specific and must be negotiated in the moment; keep it non-graphic.",
    "Never script {{user}}'s feelings, jealousy, decisions, dialogue or competitive behaviour.",
    "Do not treat one rival's loss as humiliation, punishment or a lesson she needed.",
    "No romantic or sexual framing of a rivalry that the concept establishes as unwanted.",
    "Keep hostility bounded: no coercion, stalking, sabotage of livelihood or retaliation outside the contest.",
    "Do not assume offline identity from a competitive persona — gender, age, job and appearance stay unestablished until revealed.",
    "Do not force romance, reconciliation, a decisive champion or a permanent ending."
  ],
  "diversity_axes": [
    "Domain: esports ladder, academic ranking, sales board, speedrunning, cosplay circuit, cooking, model building, card games, rhythm games, amateur sport, photography, debate, startup pitching, distance running, fandom writing or skate progression.",
    "Win condition: points, placement, time, judges' score, quota, audience vote or a private tally with no official record.",
    "History length: months, years, a decade, or a rivalry resumed after a long gap.",
    "Origin: strangers at one event, classmates, coworkers, teammates who split, mutual friends, former mentor and student, or handles only.",
    "Skill gap: dead even, one consistently ahead, alternating dominance, specialist versus generalist, or a trend line closing fast.",
    "Tone: respectful, deadpan, theatrical, icy, sportsmanlike, sibling-like, quietly obsessed or bounded hostility.",
    "Audience: none, a friend group, a niche forum, a workplace, a school cohort, a live crowd or a public leaderboard.",
    "Rules of engagement: no sabotage, silly wagers, shared footage, one private edge each, formal challenges or a full ceasefire protocol.",
    "Cooperation history: never, once, ongoing favours, forced doubles, joint projects or a shared crisis.",
    "What each envies: preparation, improvisation, consistency, peak performance, presentation, endurance, innovation or composure.",
    "Aftermath style: immediate rematch, silence, over-analysis, public grace and private fury, honest debrief or avoidance.",
    "Offline knowledge: nothing, first name only, voice only, met once, knows the job, knows the family or both assumed wrong.",
    "Romance stance: absent, possible, developing, actively unwanted or already settled and irrelevant to the contest.",
    "Setting texture: local club, university campus, corporate office, convention hall, arcade, gym, small town or fully remote.",
    "Escalation vector: promotion, public final, new category, outside challenger, rule change or a sponsor's attention."

    {
      "id": "engine",
      "label": "The rivalry engine",
      "content": "Adult {{char}} and adult {{user}} keep meeting because the same competition keeps bringing them back. The competition is the relationship's spine: it produces the calendar, the stakes, the vocabulary and most of the reasons they speak to each other. Everything else — tone, romance, history, setting — is variable around that fixed engine."
    },
    {
      "id": "classification",
      "label": "Classification test",
      "content": "A concept belongs to Friendly Rivals when removing the competition would leave essentially the same scenario. If the pair would still be interacting for the same reasons without a scoreboard, a ranking or a recurring contest, the idea belongs to another series. Keep the contest load-bearing rather than decorative."
    },
    {
      "id": "domain",
      "label": "Choosing the domain",
      "content": "Define what the domain is, what counts as winning, and how results are recorded, before defining appearance or attraction. The domain must matter to both adults independently of each other: each would still do this if the other vanished. Narrow, local and slightly absurd domains usually beat grand ones, because the stakes stay legible."
    },
    {
      "id": "character-building",
      "label": "Building each rival",
      "content": "Give each rival a method, a strength, a weakness, a history in the craft and one habit that shows up under pressure. Competence must be earned by specifics rather than asserted. {{char}} needs a life outside the competition — work, friends, money, opinions — that the rivalry complicates rather than replaces."
    },
    {
      "id": "symmetry",
      "label": "Asymmetry and fairness",
      "content": "An interesting rivalry is rarely a tie. Give one a real edge in one dimension and the other a real edge in another, then let the format decide which dimension matters today. {{char}} must be able to lose on merit, and {{user}} must be able to win without the victory being framed as a gift."
    },
    {
      "id": "record",
      "label": "Results that carry forward",
      "content": "Wins and losses should change the next interaction without ending the series. A narrow loss produces a training block, a bad joke, a changed warm-up, a new tactic. A decisive win produces awkwardness, generosity or a target on a back. Keep a running history that both characters can reference accurately."
    },
    {
      "id": "respect",
      "label": "Respect without romance",
      "content": "The respect is competitive, not romantic: it means taking the other's work seriously enough to prepare properly. Teasing, admiration, irritation and affection may all appear. Romance may be absent, possible, developing or actively unwanted, and none of those is the default."
    },
    {
      "id": "cooperation",
      "label": "Cooperation and truce",
      "content": "Rivals can help each other improve, share equipment, review footage, team up against a third party, or hold a ceasefire during a real crisis — and then return to competing. Cooperation should sharpen the rivalry rather than dissolve it, and any debt created by help should persist in the next match."
    },
    {
      "id": "identity",
      "label": "Online and offline identity",
      "content": "For remote rivalries, track what each person actually knows about the other separately: name, age, gender, appearance, job, city, voice. Long familiarity with someone's play does not imply knowledge of their life, and a wrong mental image is a legitimate engine rather than a twist to be resolved immediately."
    },
    {
      "id": "escalation",
      "label": "Escalation",
      "content": "Escalate through stakes, format, audience and access rather than through melodrama. A rematch, a promotion, a public final, a shared tournament bracket, an outside challenger or a move to a new category each raise pressure while keeping the same engine. Never escalate by making one rival suddenly cruel without setup."
    },
    {
      "id": "tone",
      "label": "Tone and register",
      "content": "Tone is a dial, not a genre: deadpan comedy, quiet professionalism, loud theatrical rivalry, icy formality and genuine warmth all work. Comedy should come from specificity, not from making the characters stupid. Whatever the register, the competition itself is treated seriously by the people doing it."
    },
    {
      "id": "boundaries",
      "label": "Boundaries and consent",
      "content": "All participants are adults. Rivalry is not consent: proximity, adrenaline, shared hotel corridors, celebrations and long history never grant access to a person. Any intimacy is activity-specific, negotiated in the moment and non-graphic on the page. {{user}}'s feelings, jealousy and decisions are never scripted."
    },
    {
      "id": "failure-modes",
      "label": "Failure modes to avoid",
      "content": "The common failures are a rival who can never be beaten, a rivalry that turns into cartoon hatred, romance treated as the inevitable reward for winning, {{user}} written as obsessed or humiliated before the scene establishes it, and sabotage used as a default plot device. Each of these collapses the engine into a different, weaker series."
    },
    {
      "id": "opening",
      "label": "Opening the scene",
      "content": "Open at a playable moment inside the competition's rhythm: a challenge issued, a leaderboard refreshed, a bracket drawn, a first offline meeting, a forced team-up or the moment one rival unexpectedly helps the other. Establish the domain and what is at stake in this meeting, then stop before anyone's reaction is decided."
    },
    {
      "id": "crossover",
      "label": "Cross-series use",
      "content": "The engine crosses well with first-meeting-offline, wrong-mental-image, forced-partnership, expert-needed and convention-community series. It crosses badly with anything that requires the pair to be isolated from other people, since a rivalry needs an audience, a record or at least a shared standard to exist."

  "raw_prompt": "Generate a non-graphic adult character-card premise for Friendly Rivals. Adult {{char}} and adult {{user}} repeatedly compete in a domain they both genuinely care about — a ranked ladder, a sales board, a speedrun category, a convention circuit, a cook-off, a debate bracket, an amateur bout, a hobby leaderboard — and the recurring contest is one of the main reasons they keep interacting. Vary the domain and win condition, the format, how long the rivalry has run, how they first met competing, the skill relationship, the tone, how public the scoreboard is, what each does better, the rules of engagement they keep, whether they have ever cooperated, what happens after a result, how much they know about each other offline, and whether romance is absent, possible, developing or unwanted. Non-negotiables: rivalry is not hostility and does not require hatred; romance is not the prize for winning; {{char}} must be able to lose on merit; competence is specific rather than asserted; sabotage is not the default; all participants are adults; rivalry is not consent and any intimacy is activity-specific and non-graphic; never script {{user}}'s feelings, decisions or competitive behaviour; keep offline identity genuinely unestablished for remote rivalries; end at a playable opening moment with the result and the relationship still open."
